title: A two-cube cubulation of the AIM free-by-cyclic example
description: An explicit finite cube complex for the exact group in AIM Question 5.2, with two three-dimensional cells and a proper cocompact CAT(0) cubical action.
plain_language: Some groups can be understood through the geometry of spaces assembled from squares and cubes. A useful arrangement has nonpositive curvature and repeats so that a finite quotient describes the entire infinite space.

This paper gives an explicit construction for one group in the AIM problem list. Its finite model has one vertex, seven edges, eight squares and two three-dimensional cubes. The face identifications and the resulting fundamental group are specified. The universal cover is the infinite CAT(0) cube complex on which the group acts freely, properly and cocompactly.

The compact description is the interesting feature. “Two cubes” counts the three-dimensional cells in a quotient that allows boundary identifications. It does not mean that every point on the boundaries of two ordinary solid cubes remains distinct.
result: Let F be the free group on a, b and c, with automorphism φ(a)=a, φ(b)=ab and φ(c)=bcb. The mapping torus uses the convention tut⁻¹=φ(u); the final b in bcb is positive.

There is a finite locally CAT(0) unit cube complex Z of dimension three, with cell counts (1,7,8,2) and fundamental group isomorphic to the full group F⋊φZ. Its universal cover carries a free, proper and cocompact action of that exact group by cubical isometries.

The finite quotient uses the general cube-complex convention allowing isometric boundary-face identifications. The stated cell counts are before subdivision; the CAT(0) universal cover satisfies the stricter embedded-cube convention.
why_it_works: A base built from two squares admits a cubical involution. A second two-square complex has infinite cyclic fundamental group and two compatible local-isometry maps into the base.

Attaching the ends of its product with an interval gives the finite quotient. The links are checked with signed edge directions and all repeated corner occurrences retained; the unique vertex link is an actual flag simplicial complex.

Reversible presentation changes identify the entire fundamental group, including the positive final b in the automorphism. Standard cubical geometry then gives the CAT(0) universal cover and the proper cocompact deck action.
A separate argument explains qualitative existence using earlier WPD, Morse and cubical-completion theorems. Those prior tools do not supply the displayed small cell counts.
limitations: The result concerns this exact marked automorphism. The workshop summary also discusses a related example with b↦aba; that formula is distinct from the b↦ab target here.
No minimum dimension, minimum cell count, virtual specialness or theorem for a whole family of free-by-cyclic groups is claimed.
The original quotient permits boundary identifications. A stricter cubical quotient can be obtained by subdivision, but the counts (1,7,8,2) then change.

The explicit construction is presented with credit to earlier geometric tools. The paper makes no historical-firstness or absolute-novelty claim, and an archived problem statement does not establish current worldwide openness.

abstract: We construct a finite locally CAT(0) unit cube complex with one vertex, seven edges, eight squares, and two three-dimensional cubes, whose fundamental group is the mapping torus of a→ a, b→ ab, c→ bcb. Its universal cover gives a proper cocompact cubical action of the exact group in AIM Question 5.2. All attaching maps, signed vertex links, and reversible presentation changes are given explicitly. We also explain a qualitative existence deduction from earlier WPD, Morse, and cubical completion theorems. The contribution presented here is the explicit small finite model; no historical firstness or minimality claim is made.
